name: Rosolane Pink
lede: Rosolane Pink is a light purplish pink from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, its name likely echoing rosolic acid, a nineteenth-century coal-tar dye, though Ridgway does not explain the link.

sections.title: A name that sounds like a dye, unconfirmed
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 plate XXVI, hue 69′, tone f, records this hue as "rosolane pink" [1]. Rosolic acid, also called aurin, was a red coal-tar dye first made in 1834 by the German chemist Friedlieb Ferdinand Runge, who named it from the German for "red oil acid" [3]. The resemblance between "rosolane" and "rosolic" is suggestive, but Ridgway's own text does not state the connection, so it is left undocumented here rather than assumed [1][3].

The ISCC-NBS 1955 revision calls this block 246, "brilliant purplish pink" [1][2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[cameo-pink]] and [[cotton-candy]], at A darker, more saturated relative in the same Ridgway plate is [[rosolane-purple|Rosolane Purple]] [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This exact pale pink is almost absent from our archive: across 23,781 paintings, only one clears our matching threshold, as photographed, a 1917 Isaac Grünewald view of Stockholm, where it covers about a fifth of the canvas [2]. A tone this pale and low-chroma rarely reads as a distinct color against varnished, aged paint, which likely explains the scarcity [2].
